subject: ELA
title: English Language Arts 7
description: A literature-rich seventh-grade course built around short stories, a classic novel, poetry, Shakespearean drama, historical fiction and high-interest nonfiction. Students write narratives, literary analyses, argumentative essays and a research paper, while weekly grammar (phrases, clauses, sentence variety, modifiers) and Greek/Latin word study are woven into the reading. Speaking and listening grow through discussions, a dramatic reading, a debate and a multimedia presentation.
framework: California Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts & Literacy; 2014 CA ELA/ELD Framework

standards.RL.7.1: Cite several pieces of textual evidence to support analysis of what a literary text says explicitly and by inference.
standards.RL.7.2: Determine a theme or central idea of a text and analyze its development; provide an objective summary.
standards.RL.7.3: Analyze how particular elements of a story or drama interact (e.g., how setting shapes characters or plot).
standards.RL.7.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases, including figurative and connotative meanings; analyze the impact of rhymes and repetitions of sounds.
standards.RL.7.5: Analyze how a drama's or poem's form or structure (e.g., soliloquy, sonnet) contributes to its meaning.
standards.RL.7.6: Analyze how an author develops and contrasts the points of view of different characters or narrators.
standards.RL.7.7: Compare and contrast a written story, drama or poem to its audio, filmed, staged or multimedia version.
standards.RL.7.9: Compare and contrast a fictional portrayal of a time, place or character and a historical account of the same period.
standards.RL.7.10: Read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas and poems, in the grades 6–8 complexity band proficiently.
standards.RI.7.1: Cite several pieces of textual evidence to support analysis of what an informational text says explicitly and by inference.
standards.RI.7.2: Determine two or more central ideas in a text and analyze their development; provide an objective summary.
standards.RI.7.3: Analyze the interactions between individuals, events and ideas in a text.
standards.RI.7.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases in informational text, including figurative, connotative and technical meanings.
standards.RI.7.5: Analyze the structure an author uses to organize a text and how major sections contribute to the whole.
standards.RI.7.6: Determine an author's point of view or purpose and analyze how the author distinguishes his or her position from others'.
standards.RI.7.7: Compare and contrast a text to an audio, video or multimedia version, analyzing each medium's portrayal of the subject.
standards.RI.7.8: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether reasoning is sound and evidence relevant and sufficient.
standards.RI.7.9: Analyze how two or more authors writing about the same topic shape their presentations by emphasizing different evidence or interpretations.
standards.RI.7.10: Read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 6–8 complexity band proficiently.
standards.W.7.1: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence, acknowledging alternate or opposing claims.
standards.W.7.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas through selection, organization and analysis of relevant content.
standards.W.7.3: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences using effective technique, relevant details and well-structured event sequences.
standards.W.7.4: Produce clear and coherent writing appropriate to task, purpose and audience.
standards.W.7.5: Develop and strengthen writing by planning, revising, editing, rewriting or trying a new approach.
standards.W.7.6: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing and link to and cite sources.
standards.W.7.7: Conduct short research projects to answer a question, drawing on several sources and generating additional focused questions.
standards.W.7.8: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources; assess credibility; quote or paraphrase while avoiding plagiarism; follow a standard citation format.
standards.W.7.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection and research.
standards.W.7.10: Write routinely over extended and shorter time frames for a range of tasks and purposes.
standards.SL.7.1: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions, building on others' ideas and expressing one's own clearly.
standards.SL.7.2: Analyze the main ideas and supporting details presented in diverse media and formats and explain how they clarify a topic.
standards.SL.7.3: Delineate a speaker's argument and specific claims, evaluating the soundness of reasoning and relevance of evidence.
standards.SL.7.4: Present claims and findings, emphasizing salient points in a focused, coherent manner with pertinent evidence, eye contact, adequate volume and clear pronunciation.
standards.SL.7.5: Include multimedia components and visual displays in presentations to clarify claims and findings.
standards.SL.7.6: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when appropriate.
standards.L.7.1a: Explain the function of phrases and clauses in general and their function in specific sentences.
standards.L.7.1b: Choose among simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences to signal differing relationships among ideas.
standards.L.7.1c: Place phrases and clauses within a sentence, recognizing and correcting misplaced and dangling modifiers.
standards.L.7.2a: Use a comma to separate coordinate adjectives.
standards.L.7.3a: Choose language that expresses ideas precisely and concisely, eliminating wordiness and redundancy.
standards.L.7.4a: Use context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
standards.L.7.4b: Use common, grade-appropriate Greek or Latin affixes and roots as clues to the meaning of a word.
standards.L.7.4c: Consult reference materials to find pronunciation and clarify precise meaning or part of speech.
standards.L.7.5a: Interpret figures of speech (e.g., literary, biblical and mythological allusions) in context.
standards.L.7.5b: Use the relationship between particular words (synonym/antonym, analogy) to better understand each.
standards.L.7.5c: Distinguish among the connotations of words with similar denotations.
standards.L.7.6: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases.

units.title: Short Stories: Conflict and Character
units.big_idea: Authors build suspense and reveal character through conflict, setting and point of view.

units.title: Novel Study: The Call of the Wild
units.big_idea: Setting and survival shape who a character becomes; themes develop across a whole novel.

units.title: Informational Reading and Argument
units.big_idea: Strong arguments rest on clear claims, relevant evidence and fair treatment of counterclaims.

units.title: Poetry: Sound, Form and Meaning
units.big_idea: Poets use sound, figurative language and form to create meaning and emotion.

units.title: Drama: A Midsummer Night's Dream
units.big_idea: Drama's structure and staging choices shape how audiences understand characters and themes.

units.title: Research Writing
units.big_idea: Researchers ask focused questions, evaluate sources and synthesize evidence ethically.

units.title: Historical Fiction: Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry
units.big_idea: Historical fiction illuminates real history; comparing it to historical accounts sharpens understanding of both.

units.title: Voices for Change: Speeches, Debate and Portfolio
units.big_idea: Speakers and writers persuade through reasoning, evidence and rhetoric; growth is shown through reflection.

weeks.topic: Launching the year; 'Thank You, Ma'am' by Langston Hughes
objectives: Analyze how characters' actions reveal traits

days.title: Reader inventory
days.work: Complete a reading interest survey, set a goal of 25 independent books for the year, and write a journal entry about a memorable story.

days.title: Read 'Thank You, Ma'am'
days.work: Read Hughes' 'Thank You, Ma'am' aloud and annotate Mrs. Jones's actions and words with sticky notes labeled 'trait' and 'evidence'.

days.title: Direct vs. indirect characterization
days.work: Build a two-column chart of direct and indirect characterization for Roger and Mrs. Jones and write a paragraph on how she changes him, citing two quotes.

days.title: Grammar: phrases vs. clauses
days.work: Learn phrases (prepositional, participial) versus independent and dependent clauses and label 15 sentences from the story.

days.title: Discussion & check
days.work: Discuss with a parent whether Mrs. Jones's choice was wise, building on each other's points, then take a short quiz on characterization and clauses.

weeks.assessment: Evidence paragraph, grammar labeling and discussion checklist.

weeks.topic: Suspense: 'The Most Dangerous Game' by Richard Connell
objectives: Analyze how setting shapes conflict and plot
Use Greek/Latin roots to define words

days.title: Ship-Trap Island
days.work: Read the first third of 'The Most Dangerous Game' and list details of setting that create a sense of danger.

days.title: Rising action
days.work: Read the middle section and chart Rainsford's three tricks on a plot diagram, noting foreshadowing clues.

days.title: Climax and ending
days.work: Finish the story and write a paragraph explaining how the jungle setting drives the conflict, with three cited details.

days.title: Word study: roots
days.work: Study roots 'mal', 'bene', 'vis/vid', 'dict' and 'port'; find story words and build a 15-word root web.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a reading quiz with two constructed responses and a 10-item root quiz.

weeks.assessment: Plot diagram, setting paragraph, reading and root quizzes.

weeks.topic: Point of view: 'The Tell-Tale Heart' by Edgar Allan Poe

days.title: Listen and read
days.work: Read along with a LibriVox recording of 'The Tell-Tale Heart' and mark every time the narrator insists he is not mad.

days.title: Unreliable narrator
days.work: Make a T-chart of what the narrator claims versus what his actions show and explain why he is unreliable.

days.title: Mood and word choice
days.work: Identify repetition, dashes and sound words that build tension and explain their effect on mood in a paragraph.

days.title: Grammar: coordinate adjectives
days.work: Learn the comma rule for coordinate adjectives (the 'and' test) and edit 12 sentences describing the old man's room.

days.title: Rewrite & check
days.work: Rewrite the climax from the police officers' point of view in 300 words and take a point-of-view quiz.

objectives: Plan and draft a personal narrative with conflict
Use dialogue, pacing and sensory detail

days.title: Finding a story
days.work: Brainstorm a 'heart map' of memorable moments and choose one with a clear conflict or turning point.

days.title: Planning
days.work: Plan the narrative on a story mountain with exposition, rising action, climax and reflection.

days.title: Drafting the opening
days.work: Draft an opening that starts with dialogue, action or a vivid setting detail, trying two versions.

days.title: Drafting the body
days.work: Finish the draft (600–900 words), slowing down the climax with sensory details and internal thoughts.

days.title: Peer conference
days.work: Read the draft aloud to a parent who gives two 'glows' and one 'grow'; record revision goals.

weeks.assessment: Complete narrative draft and revision goals.

objectives: Revise for pacing and word choice
Analyze theme in a short story

days.title: Revision: pacing
days.work: Revise the narrative using a checklist: add transitions, cut one slow section, expand the climax.

days.title: Editing & publishing
days.work: Edit for clauses, commas and spelling, then type and publish the final narrative.

days.title: Read 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi'
days.work: Read Kipling's 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi' and track how Rikki's courage develops through each conflict.

days.title: Theme statement
days.work: Write an objective summary of the story and a theme statement supported by three pieces of evidence.

days.title: Unit 1 assessment
days.work: Take a unit test on an unseen short story (CommonLit) with questions on plot, character, point of view and theme.

weeks.assessment: Published personal narrative (rubric) and unit 1 test.

weeks.topic: The Call of the Wild, chapters 1–2
objectives: Use context clues for unfamiliar words
materials: The Call of the Wild (Project Gutenberg or library)

days.title: Background: Klondike Gold Rush
days.work: Read a short article on the 1897 Klondike Gold Rush and locate Santa Clara, Seattle, Skagway and Dawson on a map.

days.title: Chapter 1
days.work: Read Chapter 1 'Into the Primitive' and list three lessons Buck learns from the man in the red sweater.

days.title: Context clues
days.work: Use context to define 10 challenging words from chapters 1–2 and check with a dictionary.

days.title: Chapter 2
days.work: Read Chapter 2 'The Law of Club and Fang' and write a journal entry on how Curly's death changes Buck.

days.title: Discussion & check
days.work: Discuss whether Buck is 'becoming worse' or 'adapting' and take a chapters 1–2 quiz.

weeks.topic: The Call of the Wild, chapters 3–4
objectives: Trace conflict between Buck and Spitz

days.title: Chapter 3
days.work: Read Chapter 3 and chart each clash between Buck and Spitz leading to their final fight.

days.title: Character tracker
days.work: Update a Buck character tracker with traits gained and lost, citing a page for each.

days.title: Grammar: sentence types
days.work: Identify simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences in a London passage, then write one of each about Buck.

days.title: Chapter 4
days.work: Read Chapter 4 'Who Has Won to Mastership' and explain how Buck leads differently than Spitz.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz on chapters 3–4 and revise five choppy sentences into compound-complex sentences.

weeks.topic: The Call of the Wild, chapters 5–6

days.title: Chapter 5
days.work: Read Chapter 5 'The Toil of Trace and Trail' and list choices Hal, Charles and Mercedes make that show ignorance.

days.title: Foils
days.work: Compare Hal's treatment of the dogs with John Thornton's in a Venn diagram and explain how they act as foils.

days.title: Connotation
days.work: Rank word sets like 'thin/skinny/gaunt/emaciated' by connotation and find London's choices in chapter 5.

days.title: Chapter 6
days.work: Read Chapter 6 'For the Love of a Man' and write about how love changes Buck.

days.title: Discussion & check
days.work: Hold a discussion on loyalty in the novel, then take a chapters 5–6 quiz.

weeks.topic: The Call of the Wild, chapter 7 and theme
objectives: Determine and trace themes across the novel

days.title: Chapter 7
days.work: Read Chapter 7 'The Sounding of the Call' and discuss the ending's meaning.

days.title: Objective summary
days.work: Write a 200-word objective summary of the whole novel without opinions.

days.title: Theme tracking
days.work: Trace a theme (survival of the fittest, nature vs. civilization or loyalty) through 6 quotations from different chapters.

days.title: Film comparison
days.work: Watch a clip from a film adaptation and note two ways it changes Buck's story and why.

days.title: Essay planning
days.work: Choose a thesis for a literary analysis essay on how setting shapes Buck and outline three body paragraphs with evidence.

objectives: Write a literary analysis with embedded quotations

days.title: Introduction
days.work: Draft an introduction with a hook, brief novel context and a clear thesis statement.

days.title: Body paragraphs
days.work: Draft three body paragraphs using claim-evidence-commentary with embedded quotations and page citations.

days.title: Conclusion & revision
days.work: Draft a conclusion and revise transitions between paragraphs for cohesion.

days.title: Editing
days.work: Edit for sentence variety, quotation punctuation and spelling, then publish the essay.

days.title: Unit 2 assessment
days.work: Take a unit test with passages from The Call of the Wild and an unseen excerpt from London's 'To Build a Fire'.

weeks.assessment: Literary analysis essay (rubric) and unit 2 test.

weeks.topic: Reading informational text: central ideas and structure
materials: ReadWorks articles on technology and teens

days.title: Text features & structure
days.work: Preview three ReadWorks articles and identify each one's structure (chronological, compare-contrast, cause-effect, problem-solution).

days.title: Two central ideas
days.work: Read an article on teen screen time and trace two central ideas through the text with a graphic organizer.

days.title: Objective summary
days.work: Write an objective summary of the article stating both central ideas and key details.

days.title: Academic vocabulary
days.work: Learn 10 academic words (analyze, significant, evidence, impact, contrast…) and use each in a sentence about the article.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz on an unseen article identifying structure and central ideas.

objectives: Evaluate evidence for relevance and sufficiency

days.title: Anatomy of an argument
days.work: Read an op-ed on a school-start-time debate and label claim, reasons, evidence and counterclaim.

days.title: Sound reasoning?
days.work: Evaluate whether each piece of evidence in the op-ed is relevant and sufficient using a rating chart.

days.title: Author's point of view
days.work: Analyze how the author distinguishes her view from opponents' using specific phrases.

days.title: Listening to arguments
days.work: Watch a short persuasive speech or ad and delineate its claims, noting any bandwagon or loaded-language fallacies.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Complete an argument-evaluation quiz on a new text.

weeks.topic: Paired texts: same topic, different authors
objectives: Compare how two authors present the same topic
materials: two articles on zoos (pro and con)

days.title: Text A
days.work: Read an article arguing zoos protect endangered species and highlight evidence types (statistics, expert, anecdote).

days.title: Text B
days.work: Read an article arguing zoos harm animals and highlight its evidence the same way.

days.title: Compare authors
days.work: Write a comparison paragraph on how each author emphasizes different evidence and facts.

days.title: Taking a position
days.work: Choose a position on 'Should zoos exist?' and fill an evidence organizer with at least 5 pieces of evidence.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Draft a claim and counterclaim statement and get feedback.

objectives: Write a claim-based essay with counterclaim and rebuttal

days.title: Introduction
days.work: Draft an introduction with background and a clear claim.

days.title: Reasons and evidence
days.work: Draft two body paragraphs, each with a reason, two pieces of cited evidence and explanation.

days.title: Counterclaim
days.work: Draft a counterclaim and rebuttal paragraph using phrases like 'Some argue… however…'.

days.title: Concise language
days.work: Cut wordiness and redundancy from 12 practice sentences, then from your own draft.

days.title: Conclusion
days.work: Draft a conclusion that restates the claim and leaves a call to action.

days.title: Revision
days.work: Revise for logical order and transitions using a color-coding check (claim, evidence, reasoning).

days.title: Editing & citations
days.work: Edit grammar and add in-text citations, then publish the final essay.

days.title: Oral argument
days.work: Deliver a 2-minute speech version of the argument with eye contact and adequate volume.

days.title: Reflection
days.work: Write a reflection on which revision made the biggest difference and why.

days.title: Unit 3 assessment
days.work: Take a unit test on an unseen argument text (claims, evidence, author's purpose, structure).

weeks.assessment: Argumentative essay (rubric), speech and unit 3 test.

weeks.topic: Sound and figurative language in poetry
objectives: Analyze rhyme, rhythm, alliteration and repetition

days.title: Rhythm and story
days.work: Read 'Paul Revere's Ride' aloud, tap the galloping meter, and mark rhyme scheme in two stanzas.

days.title: Sound devices
days.work: Annotate 'Annabel Lee' for repetition, internal rhyme and alliteration and explain how they create a haunting tone.

days.title: Extended metaphor
days.work: Analyze the staircase metaphor in Hughes' 'Mother to Son' and write what it means for life's struggles.

days.title: Allusions & analogies
days.work: Learn common mythological and biblical allusions (Achilles' heel, Pandora's box, Good Samaritan) and complete 10 word analogies.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a poetry-terms quiz and analyze an unseen short poem.

weeks.topic: Form and meaning: sonnets, free verse and Frost
objectives: Analyze how form contributes to meaning
materials: Frost: 'The Road Not Taken', 'Nothing Gold Can Stay'

days.title: The sonnet
days.work: Read Sonnet 18, map its three quatrains and couplet, and explain how the couplet turns the argument.

days.title: Frost
days.work: Read 'The Road Not Taken' and 'Nothing Gold Can Stay' and write a theme statement for each.

days.title: Free verse vs. rhyme
days.work: Compare Whitman's 'O Captain! My Captain!' with a free-verse poem and explain how form affects mood.

days.title: Poem vs. performance
days.work: Listen to a recorded reading of a poem and compare how the reader's voice changes its meaning (RL.7.7).

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a 1-page analysis of how form shapes meaning in one poem from the week.

objectives: Write original poems using devices and forms

days.title: Imagery poem
days.work: Write a free-verse poem about a place using imagery of all five senses.

days.title: Form poem
days.work: Write a sonnet, haiku sequence or ballad stanza modeled on a mentor poem.

days.title: Figurative poem
days.work: Write an extended-metaphor poem modeled on 'Mother to Son'.

days.title: Recitation practice
days.work: Memorize 14+ lines of a studied poem and rehearse with attention to pacing and emphasis.

days.title: Poetry café & semester check
days.work: Perform the memorized poem and one original poem for family, then take a semester 1 reading and grammar checkpoint.

weeks.assessment: Poetry portfolio (3 poems), recitation rubric and semester checkpoint.

weeks.topic: Shakespeare's world and Act 1 of A Midsummer Night's Dream
materials: Folger edition of A Midsummer Night's Dream

days.title: Shakespeare's world
days.work: Watch a short video on the Globe Theatre and Elizabethan England and take notes on how plays were staged.

days.title: Act 1 Scene 1
days.work: Read Act 1.1 aloud in parts and build a character map of the four lovers, Egeus and Theseus.

days.title: Shakespeare's language
days.work: Translate 10 lines into modern English using Folger notes and a dictionary for archaic words.

days.title: Act 1 Scene 2
days.work: Read Act 1.2 with the mechanicals and describe how Bottom's personality creates humor.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take an Act 1 quiz and summarize the three plotlines introduced.

weeks.assessment: Character map, translation and Act 1 quiz.

weeks.topic: Acts 2–3: the forest and the mix-ups
objectives: Analyze how setting and characters interact
Analyze how dramatic irony shapes points of view

days.title: Act 2
days.work: Read Act 2 and explain the conflict between Oberon and Titania and Puck's role.

days.title: Dramatic irony
days.work: List moments when the audience knows more than the lovers and explain how this creates comedy.

days.title: Act 3
days.work: Read Act 3 and track who loves whom on a 'love chart' before and after the potion.

days.title: Soliloquy
days.work: Analyze Helena's soliloquy at the end of Act 1 and what it reveals that dialogue does not.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take an Acts 2–3 quiz with a constructed response on dramatic irony.

objectives: Analyze how structure resolves the plot
materials: summary of Ovid's Pyramus and Thisbe

days.title: Act 4
days.work: Read Act 4 and explain how each conflict is resolved.

days.title: Pyramus and Thisbe
days.work: Read a summary of Ovid's myth and explain how Shakespeare's allusion parodies the lovers' story.

days.title: Act 5
days.work: Read Act 5 and analyze the audience's comments during the mechanicals' play.

days.title: Theme
days.work: Write a theme statement about love or imagination with three supporting quotes.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a full-play quiz on plot, structure and theme.

objectives: Compare the script to a filmed or staged version
materials: filmed version (1999 film or a recorded stage production from library)

days.title: Watch a production
days.work: Watch key scenes of a filmed production and note how costumes, setting and acting change your understanding.

days.title: Comparison essay
days.work: Write a 5-paragraph comparison of the script and film's portrayal of Bottom or Puck, citing both.

days.title: Scene rehearsal
days.work: Choose a 30-line scene, mark blocking and rehearse with family members.

days.title: Performance
days.work: Perform the scene for family using voice and gesture, then discuss interpretation choices.

days.title: Unit 5 assessment
days.work: Take a unit test on a Shakespeare excerpt with questions on language, structure and character.

weeks.assessment: Comparison essay, performance rubric and unit 5 test.

days.title: Choosing a topic

days.title: Library databases
days.work: Search the public library's student databases and find three credible sources.

days.work: Submit research question, source evaluations and working bibliography for feedback.

days.title: Paraphrase practice
days.work: Paraphrase five passages, then compare with originals to check for plagiarism.

days.work: Fix 12 sentences with misplaced and dangling modifiers, then check note cards for the same errors.

days.work: Watch a documentary clip on the topic and compare what it emphasizes versus a print source (RI.7.7).

objectives: Write an informative report integrating sources

days.title: Compare
days.work: Fill in a comparison chart of what the novel and historical sources each show about the period.

days.title: Draft
days.work: Draft a 5-paragraph essay explaining how Taylor uses or alters history and why.

days.title: Revise & edit
days.work: Revise with a checklist focused on balanced evidence from both sources, then edit.

days.title: Unit 7 assessment
days.work: Publish the essay and discuss with a parent how fiction helps us understand history.

materials: Susan B. Anthony's 'On Women's Right to Vote'
Chief Joseph's 'I Will Fight No More Forever'

days.title: Ethos, pathos, logos
days.work: Learn the three appeals and find examples in five advertisements.

days.title: Gettysburg Address
days.work: Read and listen to the Gettysburg Address and annotate parallelism and purpose.

days.title: Susan B. Anthony
days.work: Read 'On Women's Right to Vote' and trace her claims and evidence.

days.title: Chief Joseph
days.work: Read Chief Joseph's surrender speech and analyze how word choice conveys his point of view.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a paragraph comparing how two speakers use appeals and take a rhetoric quiz.

objectives: Analyze how two authors on the same topic differ
materials: paired articles on a youth issue (e.g., voting age at 16)

days.title: Paired reading
days.work: Read two articles on lowering the voting age to 16 and identify each author's claim and key evidence.

days.title: Comparison
days.work: Analyze how each author emphasizes different evidence and write a comparison paragraph.

days.title: Debate prep
days.work: Assigned a side, build a case with three reasons and evidence cards.

days.title: Anticipating rebuttals
days.work: List likely opposing arguments and draft rebuttals for each.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write and rehearse a 2-minute opening statement.

objectives: Use formal English and evidence orally

days.title: Debate rehearsal
days.work: Rehearse the opening statement and cross-examination questions with a parent.

days.title: Debate
days.work: Hold a structured debate with family (opening, rebuttal, cross-examination, closing).

days.title: Evaluate the debate
days.work: Watch a recording of the debate and evaluate both sides' reasoning with a rubric.

days.title: Persuasive speech
days.work: Write a 3-minute persuasive speech on a community issue using ethos, pathos and logos.

days.title: Deliver & check
days.work: Deliver the persuasive speech and receive rubric feedback.

objectives: Write an argument under timed conditions

days.title: Timed argument
days.work: Write a 45-minute argument essay responding to a prompt with two short sources.

days.title: Self-scoring
days.work: Score the timed essay with the rubric and revise one paragraph.

days.title: Grammar review
days.work: Complete a mixed review of phrases, clauses, sentence types, modifiers and commas.

days.title: Word study review
days.work: Review Greek/Latin roots and figurative language with a 40-item review game.

days.title: Final exam
days.work: Take the year-end ELA exam (reading passages, grammar and a short written response).

objectives: Reflect on growth as a reader and writer

days.title: Select work
days.work: Choose the best narrative, analysis, argument, research and poem pieces for the portfolio.

days.title: Revise one piece
days.work: Revise one earlier piece using everything learned this year.

days.title: Reflection letter
days.work: Write a reflection letter describing growth, challenges and goals for grade 8.

days.title: Reading celebration
days.work: Total the year's reading log and give a 3-minute book talk on the favorite book of the year.

days.title: Portfolio presentation
days.work: Present the portfolio to family, explaining one piece in depth, and create a summer reading list.
